content.prompt:
The unit circle shown has exact values.
Use the unit circle to find the exact value of these trigonometric functions.

spec.description: Unshaded unit circle with twelve exact coordinate labels, arrowed axes, two distinguished radial families and four directed angles.
spec.mathematics: The circumference points are (cos θ, sin θ) at multiples of 30°. Orange distinguishes the 30°, 150°, 210° and 330° radial family; blue distinguishes the 60°, 120°, 240° and 300° family. Directed arcs run counterclockwise from the positive x-axis to 30°, 120°, 210° and 300°.
spec.answerVisibility: All coordinates and angle annotations are permanent supplied givens. No requested part answers are printed in the diagram.

answer.worked: At $0^{\circ}$, the unit-circle point is $(1,0)$. Sine is the $y$-coordinate, so $\sin 0^{\circ}=0$.
At $0^{\circ}$, the unit-circle point is $(1,0)$. Cosine is the $x$-coordinate, so $\cos 0^{\circ}=1$.

At $0^{\circ}$, $(x,y)=(1,0)$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 0^{\circ}&=\frac01\\\tan 0^{\circ}&=0\end{align*}$$

$120^{\circ}$ is in quadrant II, where sine is positive.
$$\begin{align*}\sin 120^{\circ}&=\sin 60^{\circ}\\\sin 120^{\circ}&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$$

$120^{\circ}$ is in quadrant II, where cosine is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\cos 120^{\circ}&=-\cos 60^{\circ}\\\cos 120^{\circ}&=-\frac12\end{align*}$$

$120^{\circ}$ is in quadrant II, where tangent is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 120^{\circ}&=-\tan 60^{\circ}\\\tan 120^{\circ}&=-\sqrt3\end{align*}$$

$300^{\circ}$ is in quadrant IV, where sine is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\sin 300^{\circ}&=-\sin 60^{\circ}\\\sin 300^{\circ}&=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$$

$300^{\circ}$ is in quadrant IV, where cosine is positive.
$$\begin{align*}\cos 300^{\circ}&=\cos 60^{\circ}\\\cos 300^{\circ}&=\frac12\end{align*}$$

$300^{\circ}$ is in quadrant IV, where tangent is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 300^{\circ}&=-\tan 60^{\circ}\\\tan 300^{\circ}&=-\sqrt3\end{align*}$$

$210^{\circ}$ is in quadrant III, where cosine is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\cos 210^{\circ}&=-\cos 30^{\circ}\\\cos 210^{\circ}&=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$$

$240^{\circ}$ is in quadrant III, where sine is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\sin 240^{\circ}&=-\sin 60^{\circ}\\\sin 240^{\circ}&=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$$

$150^{\circ}$ is in quadrant II, where tangent is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 150^{\circ}&=-\tan 30^{\circ}\\\tan 150^{\circ}&=-\frac1{\sqrt3}\end{align*}$$
At $60^{\circ}$, the unit-circle point is $\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Sine is the $y$-coordinate, so $\sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
At $30^{\circ}$, the unit-circle point is $\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)$. Cosine is the $x$-coordinate, so $\cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$240^{\circ}$ is in quadrant III, where tangent is positive.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 240^{\circ}&=\tan 60^{\circ}\\\tan 240^{\circ}&=\sqrt3\end{align*}$$

$150^{\circ}$ is in quadrant II, where cosine is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\cos 150^{\circ}&=-\cos 30^{\circ}\\\cos 150^{\circ}&=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{align*}$$
At $90^{\circ}$, the unit-circle point is $(0,1)$. Cosine is the $x$-coordinate, so $\cos 90^{\circ}=0$.
At $180^{\circ}$, the unit-circle point is $(-1,0)$. Sine is the $y$-coordinate, so $\sin 180^{\circ}=0$.

$210^{\circ}$ is in quadrant III, where sine is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\sin 210^{\circ}&=-\sin 30^{\circ}\\\sin 210^{\circ}&=-\frac12\end{align*}$$

$330^{\circ}$ is in quadrant IV, where tangent is negative.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 330^{\circ}&=-\tan 30^{\circ}\\\tan 330^{\circ}&=-\frac1{\sqrt3}\end{align*}$$
At $270^{\circ}$, $(x,y)=(0,-1)$. Tangent is $y/x$, which would require division by zero. Therefore $\tan 270^{\circ}$ is undefined.

content.prompt:
The points $P,Q,R,S$ are on the unit circle. $O$ is the origin.
Find the exact coordinates of $P,Q,R,S$.

answer.worked:
On the unit circle, coordinates are $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ for the directed angle $\theta$ from the positive $x$-axis. Read each directed angle from the diagram.
$$\begin{align*}P&:\ 180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ\\P&=(\cos150^\circ,\sin150^\circ)=\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)\\Q&:\ 270^\circ-30^\circ=240^\circ\\Q&=(\cos240^\circ,\sin240^\circ)=\left(-\frac12,-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\R&:\ 360^\circ-30^\circ=330^\circ\\R&=(\cos330^\circ,\sin330^\circ)=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)\\S&:\ 90^\circ-45^\circ=45^\circ\\S&=(\cos45^\circ,\sin45^\circ)=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Use the trigonometric graphs to find the values (if they exist) of these trigonometric ratios of boundary angles.

answer.worked: The sine graph passes through $(0^{\circ},0)$, so $\sin 0^{\circ}=0$.
The cosine graph passes through $(180^{\circ},-1)$, so $\cos 180^{\circ}=-1$.
The cosine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $90^{\circ}$, so $\cos 90^{\circ}=0$.
The tangent graph passes through $(0^{\circ},0)$, so $\tan 0^{\circ}=0$.
The sine graph passes through $(90^{\circ},1)$, so $\sin 90^{\circ}=1$.
The cosine graph passes through $(0^{\circ},1)$, so $\cos 0^{\circ}=1$.
The sine graph passes through $(270^{\circ},-1)$, so $\sin 270^{\circ}=-1$.
The cosine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $270^{\circ}$, so $\cos 270^{\circ}=0$.
The sine graph crosses the horizontal axis at $180^{\circ}$, so $\sin 180^{\circ}=0$.
The tangent graph has a vertical asymptote at $270^{\circ}$. Since $\cos 270^{\circ}=0$, $\tan 270^{\circ}=\dfrac{\sin 270^{\circ}}{\cos 270^{\circ}}$ is undefined.
The tangent graph has a vertical asymptote at $90^{\circ}$. Since $\cos 90^{\circ}=0$, $\tan 90^{\circ}=\dfrac{\sin 90^{\circ}}{\cos 90^{\circ}}$ is undefined.
The tangent graph crosses the horizontal axis at $180^{\circ}$, so $\tan 180^{\circ}=0$.

answer.worked:
The diagonals $AC$ and $BE$ must have the same midpoint $D(4,2)$.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
By using the method of grouping in pairs, factorise:
$$\cos x \sin x - \cos x - \sin x + 1$$

answer.worked:
Group the terms in pairs and factorise:
$$\begin{align*}
\cos x \sin x - \cos x - \sin x + 1 &= \cos x(\sin x - 1) - 1(\sin x - 1) \\
&= (\sin x - 1)(\cos x - 1)
\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Hence or otherwise, solve the equation below for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.
$$\cos x \sin x - \cos x - \sin x + 1 = 0$$

answer.worked:
Using the factorised form from part (a):
$$\begin{align*}
(\sin x - 1)(\cos x - 1) &= 0
\end{align*}$$
Setting each factor to zero:
$$\begin{align*}
\sin x - 1 &= 0 \\
\sin x &= 1 \\
x &= \frac{\pi}{2}
\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}
\cos x - 1 &= 0 \\
\cos x &= 1 \\
x &= 0, 2\pi
\end{align*}$$
The solutions are $x = 0, \frac{\pi}{2}, 2\pi$.

content.prompt:
How many values of $x$ in the domain $0^{\circ}\leq x\leq 360^{\circ}$ satisfy the equation
$$(3\sin x-1)(\cos^2x-1)=0?$$
(A) $3$
(B) $4$
(C) $5$
(D) $6$

answer.worked:
Set each factor equal to zero.
$$\begin{align*}3\sin x-1&=0\\\sin x&=\frac{1}{3}\end{align*}$$
Sine is positive, so there are $2$ solutions (Q1 and Q2).
$$\begin{align*}\cos^2x-1&=0\\\cos x&=\pm1\end{align*}$$
This gives $x=0^{\circ},180^{\circ},360^{\circ}$, which is $3$ solutions, with no overlap.
$$2+3=5$$

content.prompt:
The diagram shows triangle $ABC$ with vertices $A(2, 2)$, $B(-4, 0)$ and $C(-4, -6)$.

Calculate the size of the obtuse angle in the triangle, correct to the nearest degree.

answer.short: $108^\circ$ (nearest degree). Use the gradient of $AB$, then add $90^\circ$ to its acute inclination.
answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the acute angle that $AB$ makes with the $x$-axis.
$$\begin{align*}
m_{AB} &= \frac{2 - 0}{2 - (-4)} \\
&= \frac{2}{6} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}
\end{align*}$$
So:
$$\begin{align*}
\tan\theta &= \frac{1}{3} \\
\theta &= \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \\
&\approx 18^\circ
\end{align*}$$
Since $BC$ is vertical, the obtuse angle at $B$ is:
$$\begin{align*}
\angle ABC &\approx 90^\circ + 18^\circ \\
&= 108^\circ
\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: If $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{9}{15}$ and $180^\circ < \theta < 360^\circ$, find the exact value of $\tan\theta$ and the possible value(s) for $\theta$ to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Since $\cos\theta=-\frac35$ and $180^\circ<\theta<360^\circ$, $\theta$ is in quadrant III.
$$\begin{align*}\sin^2\theta&=1-\left(-\frac35\right)^2=\frac{16}{25}\\\sin\theta&=-\frac45\\\tan\theta&=\frac{-4/5}{-3/5}=\frac43.\end{align*}$$
The reference angle is $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac43\right)\approx53.1301^\circ$.
$$\theta=180^\circ+\alpha\approx233.1301^\circ\approx233^\circ\quad\text{(nearest degree).}$$

content.prompt:
Which of the following statements is correct?
$$\text{A. }\forall a,b\in\mathbb{R},\quad \sin a<\sin b\Rightarrow a<b$$
$$\text{B. }\forall a,b\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right],\quad \sin a<\sin b\Rightarrow a<b$$
$$\text{C. }\forall a,b\in\mathbb{R},\quad \cos a<\cos b\Rightarrow a<b$$
$$\text{D. }\forall a,b\in[0,\pi],\quad \cos a<\cos b\Rightarrow a<b$$

answer.short: B. Sine is strictly increasing on $\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$.
answer.worked:
The sine function is strictly increasing on $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, so $\sin a<\sin b$ implies $a<b$ on this interval.
Sine is not increasing on all of $\mathbb{R}$, and cosine is decreasing on $[0,\pi]$.
Correct answer: B.

children.prompt: Show that the curves first intersect at $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$.

answer.short: First intersection: $x=\frac\pi6$, $y=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Before this point, $\cos x>\frac{\sqrt3}{2}>\sin2x$.
answer.worked:
At $x=\frac\pi6$,
$$\cos\frac\pi6=\sin\frac\pi3=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.$$
For $0\le x<\frac\pi6$, cosine decreases from $1$ towards $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and sine increases from $0$ towards $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ as its argument $2x$ increases towards $\frac\pi3$. Hence
$$\cos x>\frac{\sqrt3}{2}>\sin2x.$$
There is no earlier intersection, so the first intersection is at $x=\frac\pi6$.

content.prompt:
Which of the following is NOT an even function?

$\text{A. } f(x) = x^3\sin x$
$\text{B. } f(x) = \tan(\sin x)$
$\text{C. } f(x) = \log_e(x\tan x)$
$\text{D. } f(x) = \cos(\tan x)$

answer.short: B. $\tan(\sin x)$ is odd and not identically zero.
answer.worked:
Testing option B:
$$\begin{align*}
f(-x) &= \tan(\sin(-x)) \\
&= \tan(-\sin x) \\
&= -\tan(\sin x) \\
&= -f(x)
\end{align*}$$
So option B is odd, not even.
Correct answer: B.

classification.difficultyReason: The student must apply odd-function symmetry through a composition and distinguish a guaranteed property from possible special cases.

content.prompt:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a non-zero odd function.
Which of the functions below is also odd?
A. $f(x^2) \cos x$
B. $f(f(x))$
C. $f(x^3) \sin x$
D. $f(x^2) - f(x)$

answer.worked:
For every permitted odd function, $f(-x)=-f(x)$. For option B,
$$\begin{align*}f(f(-x))&=f(-f(x))\\&=-f(f(x)).\end{align*}$$
Thus $f(f(x))$ is necessarily odd, so the correct answer is B.
Options A and C are always even, but are not necessarily odd. In a special case either may be the zero function and therefore both even and odd; that does not make it odd for every permitted $f$. Option D is not guaranteed odd.

classification.difficultyReason: The solution count must be reframed as an interval for a parameter, with different inclusion conditions at the second and third roots.

content.prompt:
The equation $\cos px = \frac{1}{2}$ has exactly $2$ solutions where $0 \leq x \leq 2\pi$ and $p > 0$.
Find all possible values of $p$.

answer.short: $\frac56\le p<\frac76$. Include the second root and exclude the third root from $[0,2\pi]$.
answer.worked:
For the equation $\cos \theta = \frac{1}{2}$, the positive solutions for $\theta$ are:
$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}, \frac{5\pi}{3}, \frac{7\pi}{3}, \frac{11\pi}{3}, \dots$
Let $\theta = px$. Then the solutions for $x$ are:
$x = \frac{\pi}{3p}, \frac{5\pi}{3p}, \frac{7\pi}{3p}, \dots$
We need exactly $2$ solutions in the interval $0 \leq x \leq 2\pi$.
This means the second solution must be within or on the boundary of the interval, but the third solution must be strictly outside the interval.
Condition 1 (Second solution is $\leq 2\pi$):
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{5\pi}{3p} &\leq 2\pi \\
\frac{5}{3p} &\leq 2 \\
\frac{5}{6} &\leq p
\end{align*}$$
Condition 2 (Third solution is $> 2\pi$):
$$\begin{align*}
\frac{7\pi}{3p} &> 2\pi \\
\frac{7}{3p} &> 2 \\
p &< \frac{7}{6}
\end{align*}$$
Combining these two conditions, the possible values for $p$ are:
$\frac{5}{6} \leq p < \frac{7}{6}$

classification.difficultyReason: Determine two inclinations from line equations and relate them to the triangle's equal base angles.

content.prompt: A triangle is formed by the $x$-axis and the lines $5y=9x$ and $5y+9x=45$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find, correct to the nearest degree, the angles of inclination of the two lines.

answer.short: $61^{\circ}$ and $119^{\circ}$ respectively. Use $\tan\theta=m$; add $180^{\circ}$ to the negative inverse-tangent result.
answer.worked:
For $5y=9x$:
$$\begin{align*}m_1&=\frac95\\\tan\theta_1&=\frac95\\\theta_1&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac95\right)\\\theta_1&\approx61^{\circ}\end{align*}$$
For $5y+9x=45$, $y=-\frac95x+9$:
$$\begin{align*}m_2&=-\frac95\\\theta_2&=\tan^{-1}\left(-\frac95\right)+180^{\circ}\\\theta_2&\approx119^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What sort of triangle has been formed?

answer.short: Isosceles: the two interior angles at the $x$-axis are equal.
answer.worked: The left base angle is $\tan^{-1}(\frac95)$. The right base angle is $180^{\circ}-\theta_2=\tan^{-1}(\frac95)$. The base angles are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.

content.prompt: Prove, using exact values, that:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=-\sin30^\circ(-\cos30^\circ)-\cos30^\circ\sin30^\circ\\&=\sin30^\circ\cos30^\circ-\cos30^\circ\sin30^\circ\\&=\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac12\\&=0=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=\sin60^\circ\cos45^\circ+\cos60^\circ\sin45^\circ\\&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)+\frac12\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\\&=\frac{\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}+\frac1{2\sqrt2}\\&=\frac{\sqrt3+1}{2\sqrt2}=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=\frac{\sin45^\circ-(-\cos60^\circ)}{\sin45^\circ+(-\cos60^\circ)}\\&=\frac{\frac1{\sqrt2}+\frac12}{\frac1{\sqrt2}-\frac12}\\&=\frac{\frac{2+\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}}{\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}}\\&=\frac{2+\sqrt2}{2-\sqrt2}\times\frac{2+\sqrt2}{2+\sqrt2}\\&=\frac{4+4\sqrt2+2}{4-2}\\&=\frac{6+4\sqrt2}{2}\\&=3+2\sqrt2=\mathrm{RHS}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=(\sin30^\circ+0+(-\tan45^\circ))^2\\&=\left(\frac12-1\right)^2\\&=\frac14.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{RHS}&=(\sin45^\circ)^2(-\cos45^\circ)^2\\&=\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^2\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^2\\&=\frac14.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\mathrm{LHS}=\mathrm{RHS}$.

$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=\frac{\sin60^\circ}{-\tan60^\circ}-\frac{-\cos60^\circ}{\left(\frac1{-\tan45^\circ}\right)}\\&=\frac{\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)}{-\sqrt3}-\frac{\left(-\frac12\right)}{-1}\\&=-\frac12-\frac12\\&=-1.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{RHS}&=\tan^2 60^\circ-\frac1{\sin^2 30^\circ}\\&=(\sqrt3)^2-\frac1{\left(\frac12\right)^2}\\&=3-\frac1{\left(\frac14\right)}\\&=3-4\\&=-1.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\mathrm{LHS}=\mathrm{RHS}$.

[Pedagogy audit v2 · New teaching] p49 Q6 asks students to identify a cosine graph, a reflected and shifted version, and the range and period in context, which the lesson never teaches; add this before Q6.
Worked example: The graph shows the height, $H$ metres, of a paddle on a water wheel above the river bed as the wheel turns through an angle $\theta$. Find the equation of the graph.
The maximum is $18$ and the minimum is $2$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{midline}&=\frac{18+2}{2}=10\\\text{amplitude}&=\frac{18-2}{2}=8\end{align*}$$
The graph starts on the midline and falls first, so it is a reflected sine graph shifted up $10$.
$$H=10-8\sin\theta$$
Guided practice:
Proposed question: The graphs show the height, $H$ metres, of a point on a wheel as it turns through an angle $\theta$. Find the equation of each graph.
a) (with a diagram)
b) (with a diagram)
c) (with a diagram)
Answers: a) $H=9+5\cos\theta$; b) $H=10-6\cos\theta$; c) $H=6+3\sin\theta$

entries.description:
MA5-TRG-P-02 establishes and applies the properties of trigonometric functions and finds solutions to trigonometric equations

Use the unit circle to define trigonometric functions and represent them graphically
• Redefine the sine and cosine ratios in terms of the unit circle
• Verify that the tangent ratio can be expressed as a ratio of the sine and cosine ratios
• Use graphing applications to examine the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for (at least) 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, and graph the results
• Use graphing applications to examine graphs of the sine, cosine and tangent functions for angles of any magnitude, including negative angles
• Use the unit circle or graphs of trigonometric functions to establish and apply the relationships sin A = sin(180° − A), cos A = −cos(180° − A), and tan A = −tan(180° − A) for obtuse angles when 0° ≤ A ≤ 90°
• Establish and apply the relationship m = tan θ, where m is the gradient of the line and θ is the angle of inclination of a line with the x-axis on the Cartesian plane

Solve trigonometric equations using exact values and the relationships between supplementary and complementary angles
• Derive and apply the exact sine, cosine and tangent ratios for angles of 30°, 45° and 60°
• Verify and use the relationships between the sine and cosine ratios of complementary angles in right-angled triangles: sin A = cos(90° − A) and cos A = sin(90° − A)
• Find the possible acute and/or obtuse angles, given a trigonometric ratio
• Apply the sine rule and area rule to find angles involving the ambiguous case

entries.description:
We express trigonometric ratios for obtuse angles θ according to its acute reference angle A:
sin θ = sin A
cos θ = −cos A
tan θ = −tan A

To rewrite trigonometric ratios with the reference angle:
1. Find the reference angle (in Q2, A = 180° − θ).
2. Determine the sign (in Q2, sin is positive, cos and tan are negative).
3. Rewrite trig ratio with acute reference angle and the correct sign.

entries.description:
To find the acute reference angle A:
• Use the relevant inverse trigonometric function: sin⁻¹( ), cos⁻¹( ), tan⁻¹( )
• Always enter the positive value of the ratio.
• The calculator returns the acute reference angle A.

The calculator's inverse functions give results in restricted ranges that may include negative angles.
By entering the positive value, we always get a positive acute angle and this leads to fewer mistakes.
You will learn more about the inverse trigonometric functions in the Year 12 Advanced course.

entries.description:
If the question doesn’t tell you whether a triangle has an acute or obtuse angle:
1. Use sine rule to find the unknown acute angle θ.
2. Find the obtuse angle θ′ = 180° − θ.
3. Add θ′ to the given angle. If the sum > 180°, it is not a valid possibility (angle sum of triangle cannot exceed 180°).

entries.description:
We express trigonometric ratios for obtuse angles θ according to its acute reference angle A:
sin θ = sin A
cos θ = −cos A
tan θ = −tan A

To rewrite trigonometric ratios with the reference angle:
1. Find the reference angle (in Q2, A = 180° − θ).
2. Determine the sign (in Q2, sin is positive, cos and tan are negative).
3. Rewrite trig ratio with acute reference angle and the correct sign.
